title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
notes:
Task and constraints: Search for target in a rotated sorted array that may contain duplicates. Return whether the target occurs.
Idea: Use binary search. If the middle value matches, succeed. If left, middle, and right values are equal, trim both ends; otherwise identify the sorted half and keep the half whose range can contain target.
Technique and why it applies: A sorted half still supports range-based elimination, but duplicates can make the sorted side ambiguous and require cautious boundary trimming.
Invariant: If target exists, at least one possible occurrence remains inside the current interval.
Edge cases: Many equal values can force linear behavior; unlike the distinct-value version, logarithmic worst-case time is not guaranteed.
Complexity: Average time is O(log n), worst-case O(n). Extra space is O(1).
time_complexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst case
complexity_reason: Ambiguous duplicate boundaries may be removed one at a time.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II
notes:
Task and constraints: Remove every value that occurs more than once in a sorted linked list, leaving only values that appeared exactly once.
Idea: Use a dummy head and a predecessor pointer. If the next two nodes share a value, advance past the entire run; otherwise advance the predecessor by one node.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting makes every occurrence of a duplicated value contiguous, so one run can be skipped completely.
Invariant: The list before prev contains only values known to occur once; prev is the tail of that retained prefix.
Edge cases: Duplicates may start at the original head or occupy the entire list. A dummy node handles both cases uniformly.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each node is traversed a constant number of times. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The predecessor and current-run pointers traverse the list in place.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
notes:
Task and constraints: In a sorted linked list, retain one node for each distinct value and remove later duplicates.
Idea: Walk through the list. If the current node and its successor have equal values, bypass the successor; otherwise advance to the successor.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted order places duplicates next to one another, so only adjacent comparisons are needed.
Invariant: The processed prefix contains one node per distinct value and remains sorted.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node lists require no changes. Consecutive duplicate runs are removed by repeatedly checking the same current node after a bypass.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each node is visited and bypassed at most a constant number of times.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest rectangle area under a histogram of unit-width bars with non-negative heights.
Idea: Maintain indices of bars in increasing height order. When a lower bar arrives, pop taller bars and calculate the maximal width for each popped height using the new index and the previous stack top.
Technique and why it applies: The first lower bar to the right and the previous lower bar to the left bound the widest rectangle with a popped bar's height.
Invariant: Stack indices have non-decreasing heights, and each popped bar is finalized at its first lower right boundary.
Edge cases: Append a zero-height sentinel to flush the stack. Empty histograms return zero.
Complexity: Time is O(n) because each index is pushed and popped once. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Every histogram index enters and leaves the monotonic stack at most once.

title: Maximal Rectangle
approach_name: Build row heights and solve histogram
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the largest all-ones rectangle in a binary matrix.
Idea: Treat each row as the base of a histogram. Maintain heights[c], the consecutive number of ones ending at the current row, resetting a height to zero for a zero cell. For each row, calculate the largest histogram rectangle.
Technique and why it applies: Any all-ones rectangle ending at a row corresponds to a rectangle under that row's histogram heights.
Invariant: After updating a row, heights[c] equals the vertical run of ones ending at that cell.
Edge cases: Empty matrices return zero. Rows containing zeroes split possible rectangles at those columns.
Complexity: Time is O(mn), as each row's histogram is processed linearly. Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each row updates n histogram heights and performs one O(n) stack scan.

title: Partition List
approach_name: Build stable less-than and greater groups
notes:
Task and constraints: Reorder a linked list so values smaller than x appear before values at least x, preserving relative order within each group.
Idea: Build two lists with dummy heads, appending each existing node to the less-than list or the greater/equal list. Connect the first list to the second at the end.
Technique and why it applies: Separate stable passes preserve the original relative order of nodes within both partitions.
Invariant: Each partial list contains the encountered nodes of its category in original order, and each input node is placed in exactly one list.
Edge cases: Either partition may be empty. Terminate the greater/equal tail to avoid retaining an old link that forms a cycle.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1) beyond a fixed number of dummy nodes.
complexity_reason: Nodes are relinked into two stable lists using fixed pointers.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def partition(self, head: Optional[ListNode], x: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        less=ListNode(0);greater=ListNode(0);a,b=less,greater
        while head:
            nxt=head.next;head.next=None
            if head.val<x:a.next=head;a=head
            else:b.next=head;b=head
            head=nxt
        a.next=greater.next
        return less.next

title: Scramble String
notes:
Task and constraints: Decide whether one string can be transformed into another by recursively splitting a string into two non-empty parts and optionally swapping the two parts at any split.
Idea: For each pair of substrings, first compare equality and character frequencies. Try every split in both aligned and swapped arrangements; memoize each substring pair.
Technique and why it applies: Every scramble must arise from some split point, and the two recursive subproblems cover the corresponding parts in either order.
Invariant: A memoized state is true exactly when its two substrings have a valid scramble relation.
Edge cases: Unequal lengths fail immediately. Character-frequency mismatch prunes impossible states before exploring splits.
Complexity: The memoized recurrence is O(n^4) time in the straightforward substring implementation and O(n^3) states, with substring storage adding overhead.
space_complexity: O(n^3) memo states, with substring/key overhead
complexity_reason: There are O(n^3) substring pairs and each state tries O(n) splits with linear frequency checks.

title: Merge Sorted Array
notes:
Task and constraints: Merge two sorted arrays into nums1, which already has enough trailing capacity for all values. The first m entries of nums1 and all n entries of nums2 are valid inputs.
Idea: Compare the largest remaining values and write the larger one at the end of nums1, moving backward until nums2 is exhausted.
Technique and why it applies: Writing from the back avoids overwriting unread values in nums1.
Invariant: Positions after the write pointer contain the largest values from both arrays in sorted order.
Edge cases: If nums2 is empty, nums1 is already correct. If nums1's valid prefix is empty, copy all of nums2.
Complexity: Time is O(m+n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each input element is read once and output is written into nums1.

title: Gray Code
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a sequence of all n-bit Gray codes starting at zero, where adjacent values differ in exactly one bit.
Idea: For each bit width, reflect the existing sequence in reverse order and set the new high bit on each reflected value. Equivalently, value i maps to i XOR (i shifted right by one).
Technique and why it applies: The XOR formula transforms ordinary binary counting into Gray code, changing only one bit between consecutive indices.
Invariant: The sequence contains each n-bit code once and consecutive values differ in one bit.
Edge cases: n=0 conventionally yields [0], though the constraints may start at one. The sequence begins with zero.
Complexity: Time is O(2^n). Extra space is O(2^n) for the returned list.
complexity_reason: Every code is generated once and stored in the output.

title: Subsets II
approach_name: Sort and skip equal sibling choices
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all unique subsets of an array that may contain duplicate values. The empty subset is included.
Idea: Sort the array and backtrack by choosing the next element from a start index. Skip a value when it equals the previous value at the same recursion depth.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting groups duplicates, and sibling-level skipping prevents equivalent subsets while still allowing repeated values to appear in a subset.
Invariant: The path is a subset of the processed prefix, indices increase, and duplicate sibling branches are not explored.
Edge cases: An empty input returns a list containing the empty subset. Multiple equal values may still appear together if they occupy different positions.
Complexity: Time is O(n·2^n) worst case for copying subsets. Auxiliary space is O(n), excluding output.
complexity_reason: There are at most 2^n subsets and each output copy can contain n values.

title: Decode Ways
approach_name: Count decodings by one or two digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Count how many ways a digit string can be decoded when 1 through 26 represent letters A through Z. A leading zero or a zero without a valid preceding pair cannot be decoded.
Idea: Let dp[i] count decodings of the first i characters. Add dp[i-1] when the last digit is nonzero, and add dp[i-2] when the last two digits form a value from 10 through 26.
Technique and why it applies: A decoding ends with either one valid digit or one valid two-digit code, giving two disjoint predecessor cases.
Invariant: dp[i] is the number of valid decodings of the prefix ending at i.
Edge cases: An initial zero yields zero ways. A pair like 06 is invalid as a two-digit code.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(n) in this implementation.
complexity_reason: Each prefix combines at most two previous DP states.

title: Reverse Linked List II
approach_name: Reverse the selected segment in place
notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse the linked-list nodes between 1-indexed positions left and right, preserving the rest of the list.
Idea: Use a dummy node to reach the node before the segment. Repeatedly take the node after the segment's current head and insert it immediately after the predecessor, reversing the segment by head insertion.
Technique and why it applies: Each head insertion moves one node from the remaining segment to the front of the reversed prefix without changing values.
Invariant: The prefix before left is unchanged, and the segment after the predecessor is reversed incrementally while the suffix remains linked.
Edge cases: If left equals right, no change is needed. A dummy node handles reversing from the original head.
Complexity: Time is O(n) and extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each pointer update is constant-time and the selected segment is reversed in place.

title: Restore IP Addresses
notes:
Task and constraints: Insert three dots into a digit string to form all valid IPv4 addresses. Each of four segments must be between 0 and 255 and cannot have leading zeroes unless it is exactly zero.
Idea: Backtrack by selecting segment lengths one through three. Reject segments that exceed 255 or have invalid leading zeroes, and only record a result after four segments consume the whole string.
Technique and why it applies: The address has exactly four bounded segments, so recursion enumerates possible partitions while pruning invalid choices.
Invariant: The path contains valid segments and the remaining suffix has not been consumed.
Edge cases: Strings shorter than four or longer than twelve characters cannot form an address. Segment "0" is valid; "00" is not.
Complexity: The search has a small bounded branching factor and output is limited. Auxiliary space is O(1) beyond output for four segments.
space_complexity: O(1) recursion depth (four segments) plus output
complexity_reason: Only four segments are chosen and each segment has at most three digits.

title: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
notes:
Task and constraints: Return tree values in inorder order: left subtree, node, then right subtree.
Idea: Walk left while pushing nodes onto a stack. Pop the next node, record its value, then continue from its right child. Repeat until both the current node and stack are empty.
Technique and why it applies: The stack preserves ancestors whose left subtrees have been visited but whose node and right subtree remain to be processed.
Invariant: Values already emitted form the inorder traversal prefix, and the stack holds the path back to pending ancestors.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns an empty list. A skewed tree is handled without recursive call-stack depth.
Complexity: Time is O(n), since each node is pushed and popped once. Extra space is O(h) for tree height h.
complexity_reason: Each node is pushed and popped once; the stack stores at most a root-to-leaf path.

title: Unique Binary Search Trees II
approach_name: Generate roots from every split value
notes:
Task and constraints: Generate every structurally unique binary search tree containing values 1 through n, where n is at most 8.
Idea: For each value chosen as root, recursively generate all left trees from smaller values and all right trees from larger values, then combine each left/right pair under a new root.
Technique and why it applies: BST ordering uniquely partitions values into those smaller and larger than the root; every valid tree has exactly one such root choice.
Invariant: Each recursive result contains all BST shapes for its value interval, with correct ordering on both sides.
Edge cases: An empty interval returns a list containing null so a root can have an empty side. For n=1, one single-node tree is produced.
Complexity: Output is Catalan-sized and can grow exponentially; memory includes all returned tree nodes.
complexity_reason: Every root choice combines all left and right subtree possibilities.

title: Unique Binary Search Trees
notes:
Task and constraints: Count structurally unique BSTs that store the values 1 through n.
Idea: Let dp[n] be the count for n nodes. For each possible root, multiply the number of left-subtree shapes by the number of right-subtree shapes and sum over root choices.
Technique and why it applies: The root splits the remaining ordered values into independent left and right subproblems, so their counts multiply.
Invariant: dp[k] equals the number of unique BST shapes possible with k ordered values.
Edge cases: dp[0]=1 represents an empty subtree, allowing root choices with an empty side. dp[1]=1.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each node count considers every possible root split.

title: Interleaving String
approach_name: DP over prefixes of both source strings
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether s3 can be formed by interleaving s1 and s2 while preserving the order of characters from each source.
Idea: Let dp[i][j] mean the first i characters of s1 and first j of s2 can form the first i+j characters of s3. The next character may come from either source if it matches the corresponding s3 position.
Technique and why it applies: Each valid interleaving ends with a character from one of the two source strings, reducing the state to a shorter prefix.
Invariant: dp[i][j] exactly represents whether those source prefixes can form the corresponding target prefix.
Edge cases: Lengths must sum to len(s3). Empty source strings are handled by the same recurrence.
Complexity: Time and space are O(mn) in this two-dimensional version.
complexity_reason: Each pair of source-prefix lengths is computed once.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a binary tree is a valid BST, requiring every value in a node's left subtree to be strictly smaller and every value in its right subtree strictly larger.
Idea: Recursively validate each node against an exclusive lower and upper bound. The left child inherits the upper bound of the node; the right child inherits its lower bound.
Technique and why it applies: Checking only parent-child comparisons is insufficient because a descendant must satisfy every ancestor's ordering constraint.
Invariant: Every node in a recursive subtree must lie strictly within the bounds imposed by all its ancestors.
Edge cases: Empty trees are valid. Use bounds beyond the integer range in Java so minimum and maximum int values are handled correctly.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion depth.
complexity_reason: Each node is checked once with inherited bounds.

Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for recursion depth.
complexity_reason: Each node is checked once with inherited bounds.

title: Recover Binary Search Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Two node values in an otherwise valid BST have been swapped. Restore the tree without changing its structure.
Idea: Inorder traversal of a valid BST is sorted. Find the first node before an inversion and update the second node whenever a later value is smaller than its predecessor; swap those two values after traversal.
Technique and why it applies: Two swapped values create one or two inversions in the inorder sequence, revealing the misplaced nodes.
Invariant: The traversal records the earliest larger predecessor and the latest smaller successor implicated by inversions.
Edge cases: Adjacent swapped values create one inversion; non-adjacent values create two. The problem guarantees exactly two values are swapped.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(h) for the traversal stack or recursion.
complexity_reason: Inorder traversal visits each node once and stores a root-to-leaf stack.

title: Same Tree
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether two binary trees have identical structure and equal values at corresponding positions.
Idea: If both nodes are null, the subtrees match. If exactly one is null or values differ, they do not match. Otherwise recursively compare left children and right children.
Technique and why it applies: Tree equality requires matching both the root value and the structure and values of both corresponding subtrees.
Invariant: A recursive comparison returns true exactly when the two subtrees rooted at the current nodes are identical.
Edge cases: Two empty trees are equal. A missing child in only one tree makes the structures different even if all present values match.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for the number of corresponding nodes examined. Extra space is O(h) for recursion depth.
complexity_reason: Each corresponding node pair is compared once.
